title: Children's Oral Narrative Skills Through the Lens of Internal State Terms: A Large-Scale Study of Fictional Stories Elicited With the Multilingual Assessment Instrument for Narratives
abstract: Purpose: This article investigates the development of oral narrative skills in children through the lens of internal states in a large cross-linguistic data set of comparable fictional stories. Method: In a joint effort of research groups around the world, 5,507 picture-based stories were elicited from 2,763 monolingual and bilingual typically developing (TD) children aged 3–13 years in 32 countries across 44 languages with the Multilingual Assessment Instrument for Narratives (MAIN; Gagarina et al., 2019 ). These were transcribed and coded for internal state terms (ISTs) that express story characters' thoughts, emotions, and perceptions. Using generalized mixed models, we investigated the likelihood of a child producing ISTs in the stories, as influenced by age, monolingualism versus bilingualism, and, for bilinguals, first language versus second language, elicitation mode (telling vs. retelling), IST type, story type, and story length. Results: We found strong positive effects of age and elicitation mode (retelling) on IST production, but no differences between monolinguals and bilinguals or for bilinguals in their two languages. title: Integrating an Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) Literacy Feature Into Shared Storybook Reading for Autistic Children Who Need or Rely on AAC
abstract: Purpose: This study explored the impact of integrating an augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) literacy feature (Transition to Literacy [T2L] initial-letter sound feature), adapted to target letter–sound correspondence, within a grid-based AAC topic display on the accuracy of letter–sound correspondence identification by children with autism or autism-like characteristics who need or rely on AAC. Method: The study used a multiple-baseline-across-participants single-case experimental design with six participants ages 5–10 years, who had limited or no letter–sound correspondence knowledge (two or fewer letter sounds). Results: All participants demonstrated increased accuracy in identifying target letter sounds from baseline to intervention, although with variability within and across participants. All participants generalized gains from identifying individual letter sounds to identifying initial-letter sounds in written consonant–vowel–consonant words. Conclusions: Results suggest that interacting with the adapted T2L initial-letter sound feature can support increased letter–sound correspondence knowledge. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Hidden Barriers in Inclusive Classrooms: Teachers' Perceptions and Students' Experiences of Participation With Hearing Loss
abstract: Purpose: This study examined how general education teachers perceive the school participation of students with hearing loss in mainstream classrooms and which factors they identify as facilitating or hindering participation. A second aim was to compare teachers' perspectives with students' own accounts to identify convergences and divergences in perceived participation, thereby revealing hidden barriers and informing inclusive practice. Method: A qualitative, descriptive design was employed to capture in-depth insights into participants' lived experiences. Data were collected through semistructured interviews with 25 general education teachers (21 women, four men) from 19 mainstream schools in Germany. Teachers' perspectives were analyzed using thematic analysis and systematically compared with previously collected qualitative data from students with hearing loss. Results: Teachers generally reported positive attitudes toward inclusion and emphasized supportive relationship and strategies such as clear communication and classroom adaptions. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: When Language Access Is at Risk: Children of Parents With Deafblindness and the Role of Societal Support
abstract: Purpose: This commentary emphasizes the child's position and the right to develop language that enables communication with a parent who has deafblindness. We argue that societal services have a responsibility to ensure that this right is fulfilled. Deafblindness affects access to information and communication and has implications for family life when a parent has deafblindness. In such families, shared communication is essential for emotional bonds, parenting, and children's development, yet it often requires adaptations beyond spoken or visual sign language, including tactile and social haptic and other forms of communication. Method: This commentary is based on a research project on family life and health in families where a parent has deafblindness and is grounded in the Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, in which we emphasize societal responsibility for supporting children's language development. Result: The argument of the right for the child to develop language that enables communication with a parent with deafblindness and the responsibility of societal services is illustrated in the Swedish context. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Development and Validation of an International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health–Based Communication Screening Scale for Preschool Children
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to develop and validate the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF)–based Communication Screening Scale (CSS) for monolingual Turkish-speaking preschool children, grounded in the ICF framework and based on parent report. Method: The item pool was generated from 54 ICF second-level codes, reviewed by experts, and refined through content validity analysis and a pilot study. The final 41-item draft was administered to 210 children (105 with speech and/or language disorders, 105 typically developing peers) 36–72 months of age and one of their parents. For validation, the Turkish Early Language Development Test, the Ankara Articulation Test (AAT), and the Turkish version of the Focus on the Outcomes of Communication Under Six–34 (FOCUS-34-TR) were used. Results: Factor analysis yielded a 23-item scale with four subfactors: language skills, communication, speech intelligibility, and attention. Known-groups validity demonstrated that the scale significantly differentiated children with and without disorders, except for the attention factor. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Children's Rights to the Best Possible Care: Establishing Processes for Data Collection in Routine Care to Address Questions of Intervention Effectiveness for Children With Speech Sound Disorder
abstract: Purpose: The United Nations Convention of the Rights of the Child (CRC) recognizes that all children have a right to the best possible care, CRC Article 24 (health, water, food, environment). For children with speech sound disorder, this is vital in order to protect their rights to CRC Article 13 (sharing thoughts freely), CRC Article 19 (protection from violence), and CRC Article 28 (access to education). Determining what constitutes best possible care for this population is challenging because much evidence for intervention takes place outside of routine care. This review article provides an overview of Phase 1 of the Maximising the Impact of Speech and Language Therapy for Children with Speech Sound Disorder (MISLToe_SSD) program of research, which ultimately aims to establish a process for using data collected in routine care to investigate best possible care for children with speech sound disorder. The purpose of Phase 1 was to obtain consensus on a diagnostic pathway, a defined list of interventions, and a core outcome set. title: Personal Narrative Assessment to Guide Clinical Practices in the Assessment and Support of Children With Developmental Language Disorder: A Tutorial
abstract: Purpose: This tutorial demonstrates how personal narratives elicited using the Global TALES (Talking About Lived Experiences in Stories) protocol can be analyzed using the four components of the Linguistic Underpinnings of Narrative in Aphasia (LUNA) framework for discourse analysis—pragmatics, macrostructure planning, propositional, and linguistic—in clinical practice to assess the language and communication skills of children with developmental language disorder (DLD). Such analysis can support diagnostic decision making or identification and monitoring of intervention goals related to the child's needs. Language measures that can be applied and interpreted in clinical practice are presented and linked to each of the four components of the LUNA framework. By understanding which measures correspond to these components, clinicians can identify the child's strengths and challenges across the four components to obtain a more complete view of the child's oral narrative production skills. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Universal Design for Learning With Preschoolers Who Are Deafblind: Promoting Communication and Language Development
abstract: Purpose: Preschoolers who are deafblind are a low-incidence and heterogeneous group. Consequently, many speech-language pathologists (SLPs) may not have encountered these children. However, SLPs are essential members of the educational team serving a child who is deafblind. Collaboration is necessary to address the child's unique strengths, type and degree of visual impairment and hearing loss, accompanying disabilities, and learning needs. Universal Design for Learning (UDL) provides a flexible approach to enhance collaboration that promotes the child's access to and development of social interaction, communication, and language. Conclusion: This article (a) identifies relevant current research on the effectiveness of UDL, (b) explores UDL principles as a vehicle for facilitating the SLP's collaboration with the child's family and other educational team members, and (c) outlines how UDL principles support the SLP's role with preschoolers who are deafblind.

journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Honoring Children's Communication Rights: Listening to the Perspectives of Children Who Stutter Using Drawings, Self-Report Measures, and Interviews
abstract: Purpose: Reflecting a commitment to the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), and Articles 12 (respect for children's views) and Article 13 (sharing thoughts freely) in particular, this study aimed to explore whether drawings with interviews are a suitable method for understanding the perspectives of children who stutter (CWS) and what CWS communicate about their talking using this method. Method: Data were collected with 16 children aged 4;0 (years;months)–6;10 and involved drawings (62), interviews, and three self-report measures. The drawings were analyzed quantitatively across two dimensions: (a) developmental analysis and (b) focal point analysis. Inductive reflexive thematic analysis of the interview transcripts was also conducted. Results: Self-report measure scores indicated that most participants were “happy” about their talking with an average self-perception of little/no difficulty when talking. Participants demonstrated developmentally age-appropriate drawing skills. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Developmental Patterns in Deaf Children's Signed Composition Across Narrative, Informational, and Opinion Genres
abstract: Purpose: This study examined developmental change in macrostructural (discourse-level) signed composition among deaf children over the course of one academic year. The study also investigated whether grade level, early language access, and demographic characteristics were associated with differences in change across narrative, informational, and opinion genres. Method: Participants included 181 deaf children from prekindergarten through third grade enrolled in 11 signing programs in the United States. Children produced self-generated signed compositions in narrative, informational, and opinion genres at the beginning and end of the academic year. Linear mixed-effects models were used to examine fall-to-spring changes in discourse organization while accounting for grade level and child-level characteristics. A lexical unit count was also recorded for each composition as an index of signed language productivity. Results: Children demonstrated growth in discourse organization across all three genres during the school year. Grade level emerged as a stronger predictor of change than chronological age. title: Alignment of Parent and Child Self-Report of Bilingual Language Experience and Proficiency
abstract: Introduction: Information pertaining to language experience and proficiency is crucial in studies of bilingual children and is usually sought from parents. However, there are barriers to obtaining valid information from parents, which may be addressed by child's self-report. In this study, we examined the relationships between parent report and child self-report, including whether relationships differ by child's grade level. Method: Parent and child questionnaires were analyzed from n = 489 Spanish/English bilinguals in prekindergarten through third grade ( M age = 7.24). Both questionnaires resulted in measures of proficiency in Spanish and English as well as bilingual experience. Results: Child questionnaires administered directly to the child yielded higher response rates (93%) than questionnaires sent home for parents (31%). Correlations between similar indicators of proficiency and experience across child and parent reporters ranged from medium to large. Multiple regression analyses revealed that grade level was a significant predictor of child's self-reported proficiency in both languages but not of bilingual experience. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Estimated Prevalence of Developmental Language Disorder Risk in West Virginia Schools
abstract: Purpose: Developmental language disorder (DLD) is linked to long-term academic and social difficulties. Despite these lasting impacts, state-level prevalence estimates are limited. This study estimated prevalence among early-elementary students in West Virginia who may be at risk for DLD and examined variation by grade, locale, and assessment instrument. Method: A cross-sectional screening battery was administered to 252 students in Grades 1–2 across six Title I schools. Children with Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test–Second Edition Matrices standard scores ≤ 70 were excluded prior to analysis. A dual-criterion definition of DLD risk was used: ≤ 80 on the Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals–Fifth Edition (CELF-5) core composite and ≤ 92 on the Test of Narrative Language–Second Edition (TNL-2). Descriptive statistics and mixed-effects logistic regression (random intercept for school) tested effects of grade, gender, and locale. Results: Using the dual-criterion definition, 72 of 252 students (28.6%) met criteria for being at risk for DLD. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Promoting Children's Rights Through Breastfeeding Support: A Randomized Controlled Trial of a Speech-Language Pathologist–Led Intervention Among Migrant Mothers in Primary Health Care
abstract: Purpose: This randomized controlled trial evaluated a culturally adapted breastfeeding intervention led by speech-language pathologists (SLPs) for migrant mothers, grounded in the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC). The intervention addressed the rights to nondiscrimination (CRC Article 2), best interests of the child (CRC Article 3), survival and development (CRC Article 6), highest attainable standard of health (CRC Article 24), full potential (CRC Article 29), and cultural identity (CRC Article 30). The study examined whether the intervention improved exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) duration, maternal self-efficacy, infant oral-motor function, and maternal postpartum quality of life (MAPP-QOL). Method: Seventy-four migrant women in Portugal were randomly assigned to an intervention group (IG; n = 37) receiving culturally adapted, SLP-led breastfeeding support or a control group ( n = 37) receiving standard care. The intervention included a prenatal workshop, early feeding assessment, and individualized SLP counseling. title: Upholding Children's Communication Rights by Ensuring Access to Full and Appropriate Language Assessments and Corresponding Evidence-Based Interventions
abstract: Purpose: This commentary is motivated by Articles 23 (children with disabilities) and 28 (right to education) of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC). Article 23 upholds the rights of children to education and training, leading to “the fullest possible social integration and individual development. … ” A key component of social integration and individual development, and thus a key target of education and training, is communication and literacy skills. Article 28, indeed, includes combating illiteracy via evidence-based teaching methods. Also informing this commentary is Article 12 (respect for children's views). Background: Some children have communication impairments that impede their ability to fully realize their rights to social integration and individual development. We address the needs of these individuals to full and appropriate language assessments and corresponding evidence-based interventions. Our focus is on symbolic language, a type of language that comprises abstract symbols and rules for combining these symbols into phrases and sentences (e.g., spoken English, written Spanish, or Chinese Sign Language). title: The Effect of Phonology and Semantics on Reading and Memorizing Written Sentences in Chinese Prelinguistic Deaf People
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to investigate the processing differences of phonological interference (tongue twisters) and semantic interference (subject–object interchange/double-object interchange) between prelingual deaf Chinese speakers and normal-hearing speakers during sentence reading and memory, to test the deficit phonemic awareness hypothesis and the deficit structure awareness hypothesis of deaf reading, and to provide theoretical basis for deaf education strategies. Method: Twenty-two prelingually deaf college students (hearing loss ≥ 85 dB) and 41 normal-hearing college students (including 22 ability-matched groups) were recruited. Thirty-two sets of experimental sentences (normal correct sentences, normal incorrect sentences, tongue-twister correct sentences, tongue-twister incorrect sentences) were used. We used a two-phase experimental task. In the first (reading) phase, participants read each sentence and performed a sentence logic judgment task. In the second (memory) phase, after an arithmetic interference task, participants completed a fill-in-the-blank recall task. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Spelling Errors of Monolingual English-Speaking Students and Spanish-Speaking Bilingual Learners
abstract: Purpose: This study examined the types of spelling errors produced by typically developing bilingual learners (BLs) and monolingual English-speaking students and investigated whether students' vocabulary knowledge predicted the rate of spelling errors. Method: Writing samples were collected from 100 fifth-grade students (50 Spanish-speaking BLs and 50 monolingual English speakers) during an authentic classroom writing assessment. Spelling errors were coded based on English phonology, orthography, and morphology. A simple linear regression examined the relation between students' vocabulary knowledge, measured by a standardized vocabulary task, and their total number of error codes. Results: Only the proportion of whole-root morpheme substitution errors differed significantly between groups, with monolingual English-speaking students producing a higher proportion of these errors. Students' vocabulary knowledge significantly predicted their total number of errors, with higher vocabulary knowledge associated with fewer spelling errors. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Phonological Awareness of Dyslexic Jordanian Arabic–Speaking Children: The Role of Diglossia
abstract: Purpose: This study examines the impact of diglossia on the phonological awareness of dyslexic Jordanian Arabic–speaking children, focusing on deletion, segmentation, and reading tasks in both Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and Colloquial Arabic (CA). Method: Forty dyslexic and 40 typically developing (TD) children from special education resource rooms in four private schools in Amman, Jordan, participated. Results: Statistical analysis revealed that both groups performed better in MSA than in CA across all tasks, with TD children outperforming dyslexic children and task difficulty decreasing with grade level. Dyslexic children found segmentation easier than deletion, whereas TD children found both tasks equally challenging. A significant relationship was observed between reading and deletion tasks in CA for second-grade TD children and in MSA for second-grade dyslexic children. Conclusions: MSA–CA performance gap should inform instructional strategies, suggesting that phonological awareness interventions need to target the weaker variety (CA) while maintaining support in MSA. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Children's Communication and Rights: Global Cleft Care in Relation to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this article was to examine the application of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) to the human and communication rights of children with cleft lip and palate (CLP). The authors of this article, some of whom also have lived experience of CLP, are clinicians and researchers who work with children who have CLP. In this article, the authors provide several examples of initiatives and research around the globe that have supported children with CLP and align with the CRC. Conclusion: Providers who work with people with CLP from birth through young adulthood have helped to support the CRC through various programs that have addressed the United Nations: Article 2 (nondiscrimination), Article 6 (life, survival, and development), Article 12 (respect for the views of the child), Article 13 (freedom of expression), Article 23 (children with a disability), Article 24 (health and health services), Article 27 (adequate standard of living), Article 28 (access to education), Article 29 (goals of education), and Article 30 (children from minority or indigenous groups). title: Sentence Composition Instruction With Language Supports for a Fifth Grader With a Learning Disability: A Pilot Study
abstract: Purpose: Writing interventions for elementary-grade students with learning disabilities have traditionally focused on paragraph-level strategies ( McMaster et al., 2018 ). Students who struggle to compose a complete sentence need more explicit instruction and may benefit from additional language and self-regulation supports ( Kim & Graham, 2022 ). The purpose of this pilot study was to investigate the effect of a sentence writing intervention on the writing of a fifth-grade student with a learning disability. Method: This pilot study used an exploratory AB single-case design to measure the effects of a sentence writing intervention on the writing of a fifth-grade boy with a learning disability. The participant received 10 daily sentence writing lessons focusing on writing complete sentences with adjectives to describe pictures. Supports included steps for planning a sentence, a self-checklist for evaluation, and word banks. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Children's Communication Rights in the Holistic Assessment of Speech Sound Disorders: Do Speech-Language Pathologists Use the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health Framework?
abstract: Purpose: During the assessment process, speech-language pathologists (SLPs) have the opportunity to account for the involvement, thoughts, and views of children with speech sound disorders (SSDs). This is in alignment with the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC; UNICEF, n.d.; United Nations, 1989) including CRC Article 12 (Respect for children's views), Article 13 (Sharing thoughts freely), and Article 23 (Children with disabilities), which affirms SLPs' role to facilitate participation and consider perspectives. The International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF; World Health Organization, 2001) offers a holistic framework that can guide assessment practices, including accounting for children's views of their own speech. While previous research has been limited to theoretical application, the current study provides preliminary data regarding how American SLPs practically utilize the ICF framework in the evaluation of children with SSDs. Method: An online survey was created using REDCap and disseminated to currently practicing SLPs across the United States. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Upholding Young Children's Right to Child Protection Through Quality Relationships and Policy
abstract: Purpose: Children's rights to protection and participation, as outlined in the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, Article 3 (Best interest of the child), Article 12 (Respect for children's views), and Article 19 (Protection from violence), must be upheld, and education and health professionals working with children hold a critical role in ensuring these rights are protected. Infants and children with disabilities are especially vulnerable to maltreatment, representing a significant proportion of abuse cases. Children who use diverse communication styles often face additional barriers when expressing concerns or reporting harm, increasing their risk of harm when adults fail to recognize or respond to their communication effectively. This article advocates for education and health professionals to create a culture of safety that enables children to express their safety and well-being concerns through recognition of their diverse communication styles as expressions of their agency and rights. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: A Comparison of Internal State Verb Production in Fictional and Personal Narratives Elicited via Multilingual Assessment Instrument of Narratives and Global Talking About Lived Experiences in Stories
abstract: Purpose: Internal state verbs and verb constructions (ISVs) play a central role in representing internal states, such as feelings or intentions, and are therefore frequently used when narrating fictional or personal narratives. This study aimed to compare the use of ISVs in German-speaking preschoolers across five ISV categories in two narrative genres: fictional and personal narratives. Method: Twenty-one typically developing German-speaking preschoolers, ages 4;3 (years;months) to 7;0, produced two fictional narratives, consisting of three episodes each, elicited via the Multilingual Assessment Instrument of Narratives (MAIN), and six personal narratives using the Global TALES (Talking About Lived Experiences in Stories) protocol. The presentation of the tasks was counterbalanced. ISVs were classified into five categories of internal states (experiential, emotional, motivational, cognitive, and socio-relational). The relative use of ISV types and tokens per story was analyzed. Regression models were fitted as Bayesian multilevel binomial models. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Professional Development and Implementation of Learning: A Survey of Speech-Language Pathologists Providing Services to Adolescents With Developmental Language Disorder
abstract: Purpose: Developmental language disorder (DLD) is a hidden disorder in understanding and producing language, which has lifelong impacts. There is a significant amount of research-based evidence to support speech-language pathologists (SLPs) who support younger children with DLD, yet there is a dearth of professional development (PD) specific to intervention for older students and implementation of research in practice. Method: We distributed a 26-question survey to SLPs working with adolescents (i.e., children in Grades 5 and above) who have DLD via American Speech-Language-Hearing Association groups, social media, and researcher connections. Survey questions asked about their perceptions of (a) available PD opportunities, (b) confidence in learning and applying new strategies, and (c) PD delivery. Results: We analyzed data from 117 complete surveys using descriptive statistics. SLPs who responded to this survey sought PD most often through online platforms and live conferences. Respondents reported difficulty finding PD specific to serving older students with DLD. title: Spelling Outcomes in Adolescents and Young Adults With Childhood Apraxia of Speech Reveal Persistent Linguistic Deficits
abstract: Purpose: The aim of this study was to characterize sources of variability in spelling performance in adolescents and young adults with a history of childhood apraxia of speech (CAS), including linguistic skills, motor–speech sequencing, spelling error types, and residual speech errors. We also examined whether selected endophenotypes differ from peers with a history of speech sound disorder without CAS (SSD-no CAS). Method: Correlations assessed relations among single-word decoding, oral language, phonological awareness, syllable sequencing, and spelling in participants with a history of CAS ( N = 32; ages 12;6–25;3 [years;months]). Linear regression, including an interaction term for the effect of group by endophenotype, was used to compare the spelling performance of participants with a history of CAS with age-matched peers with a history of SSD-no CAS ( N = 32; ages 12;1–25;1 [years;months]), using the same endophenotypes. Spelling errors were classified by linguistic type using the Spelling Sensitivity System (SSS), and persistent speech errors were examined in relation to spelling. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Early Language and Mental Health Cascades in Preadolescents With and Without History of Late Talking
abstract: Purpose: This study compared mental health outcomes in preadolescents with and without a history of late talking (HLT) to determine whether outcomes cascade from early language ability, considering ecological and early mental health factors. Method: We included 52 Mandarin-speaking preadolescents (100% Han Chinese) 9–11 years of age: 26 with HLT ( M = 10.15 years, SD = 0.34; 20 boys, six girls) and 26 without HLT ( M = 10.20 years, SD = 0.38; 17 boys, nine girls). Both groups had comparable nonverbal cognitive abilities ( p = .721). The mental health outcomes assessed, based on parents' reports and participants' performance in laboratory tasks, included conceptual learning for adaptation, competence and emotion, self-regulation, and autism-like characteristics. Early language ability was assessed during toddlerhood (24–32 months of age) and the preschool period (48–57 months of age). Results: Preadolescents with HLT performed worse in conceptual learning, self-regulation, and social functioning than those without HLT ( η p 2 s = .08–.20), indicating medium-to-large effect sizes. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Assessment and Intervention of Letter Knowledge With Children With Developmental Language Disorder: A Systematic Review
abstract: Purpose: Letter knowledge, including letter-name and letter-sound recognition and identification, and writing, is foundational for decoding and reading development. Children with developmental language disorder (DLD) are at risk for persistent literacy difficulties; however, assessment and intervention practices for this population remain underexplored. This systematic review synthesizes research on letter-knowledge assessment and intervention in children with DLD. Method: Studies examining English-language assessment or intervention of letter knowledge among children aged 3–18 years with DLD or specific language impairment were systematically identified across multiple databases. Two reviewers independently screened all studies and extracted data using a standardized protocol. A narrative synthesis summarized patterns in assessment focus, intervention, and instructional approaches. Results: Assessment studies most often examined letter-name and letter-sound identification, while recognition and writing tasks were rarely included. Only one study assessed all five subskills. title: Applying the Convention on the Rights of the Child Through the Inter-American System: Advancing Communication Rights for U.S. Children With Communication Disorders
abstract: Purpose: In this article, we examine how the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights' (IACHR) 2025 report, The situation of the rights of persons with disabilities in the Americas , serves as a mechanism for incorporating principles from the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) to improve treatment outcomes for children with communication disorders in the United States, by integrating child-centered and rights-based principles into national policy and clinical practice, in the context of U.S. nonratification of the CRC. Method: Using a legal-analytical method grounded in treaty interpretation, comparative law, and policy analysis, we examine the IACHR's recommendations and the CRC's key provisions (Articles 2, 3, 6, 12, 13, 23, and 28) alongside U.S. disability law, including the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act. We situate communication as a fundamental human right and identify operational strategies derived from the CRC across three domains: early intervention, inclusive education, and communication access in schools. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Understanding Deafblindness: The Foundation for Successful Communication Intervention
abstract: Purpose: This tutorial provides speech-language pathologists (SLPs) with foundational knowledge to support their communication interventions with children and youth who are deafblind. This is a small disability group of great heterogeneity, with most having some functional vision and/or hearing and additional disabilities. The impact of deafblindness cannot be understood by adding the impacts of the child's hearing loss and visual impairment, as these senses frequently interact as the two distance senses for learning. Deafblindness greatly reduces both observational and incidental learning, necessitating the crafting of experiences and direct teaching of concepts. Children who are deafblind learn through the parts-to-whole approach, experiencing part of a context or experience and then needing the support of a trusted other to guide meaning-making. Receptive and expressive communication is often multimodal. Method: This tutorial provides a foundation on deafblindness, including a focus on learning and cognitive development, communication development, communication assessment, literacy development, and evidence-based practices and professional competencies. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: A Survey of Speech-Language Pathologists' Current Clinical Practices in Setting Mastery Criteria
abstract: Purpose: Little is known about the mastery criteria that school-based speech-language pathologists (SLPs) select when writing therapeutic goals. This survey study aimed to document the criteria used, determine how data are collected by school-based SLPs, and examine the underlying reasons for the criteria used. Method: This mixed-methods survey study recruited school-based SLPs in the United States via social media and e-mail to complete an online questionnaire of up to 16 items examining mastery criteria, data collection practices, and underlying rationales. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, and open-ended responses were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results: One hundred twenty-five school-based SLPs completed the survey. The majority of respondents reported that they used a mastery criterion of 80% accuracy across three sessions. The most frequently cited reason was the belief that their chosen criteria would promote generalization and long-term retention. Trial-by-trial continuous data collection was the most common data collection method. Conclusions: Findings revealed a reliance on familiar mastery thresholds, despite emerging evidence

title: Parental Involvement, Gender Ideologies, and Socioeconomic Factors: Implications for Early Language Development in Preschool-Aged Children
abstract: Purpose: Research suggests that increased paternal involvement in childrearing has a positive effect on child development. However, there is a lack of knowledge about the role of fathers in their children's language development. The current study aimed to analyze the impact of parental involvement on language development of preschool children. It used a cross-sectional, correlational design to investigate the associations between parental involvement, particularly in language-promoting activities, and young children's language development, while also considering the role of parental gender ideologies and sociodemographic factors. Data were collected from 150 parents (fathers and mothers) and 80 children (average age of 47.35 ± 6.85 months), and two-family arrangements were compared. Parents completed extensive questionnaires, and children's linguistic skills were assessed using the European–Portuguese Preschool Language Assessment. The findings show that parental involvement, namely, reading to preschool children by both fathers and mothers, contributes significantly to their linguistic development, although in different ways. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Clinical Focus: Clinical Applications of the Global TALES (Talking About Lived Experiences in Stories) Protocol for Assessment of Personal Event Narrative Language
abstract: Purpose: Personal event narratives are a universal form of discourse across cultures and languages. Developing the ability to share personal event narratives supports friendships, classroom participation, academic success, and vocational outcomes. Global TALES (Talking About Lived Experiences in Stories) is a free-access protocol with scripted prompts based on emotions and experienced events, designed to elicit personal event narratives from children and adolescents. This clinical focus article provides guidelines for the use of Global TALES in multilingual contexts, including careful translation/adaptation of the protocol, principles and methods of dynamic assessment, and procedures for analysis of personal narrative samples. Method: The authors reviewed literature focused on the contribution of personal event narrative language to a comprehensive language assessment and intervention plan. Results explain optimal linguistic and cultural adaptation procedures applicable to the Global TALES protocol, considerations when collaborating with interpreters, administration of dynamic assessment methods compatible with eliciting and evaluating narrative language, and language sample analys

journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Supporting Language Sample Analysis in Practice Using the Active Implementation Frameworks
abstract: Purpose: Formalized language sample analysis (LSA), which uses standardized protocols and validated, software-supported transcription and analysis methods, is an evidence-based approach to assessing spoken language disorders. However, most school-based speech-language pathologists (SLPs) have reported that system-level barriers substantially limit their ability to use formalized LSA. This study applied the Active Implementation Frameworks to evaluate how guided implementation supports may promote the uptake of formalized LSA among school-based SLPs and to examine their effects on key implementation outcomes. Method: SLPs were assigned to a guided implementation group (training, services, and expert-facilitated discussion) or a self-directed group (free resources only). Using a convergent mixed-methods design, we assessed fidelity, acceptability, adoption, and appropriateness. Results: SLPs in the guided group demonstrated high fidelity and rated implementation supports as acceptable. Adoption of formalized LSA increased from 0% to 100% in the guided group, compared to a modest increase in the self-directed group. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Veahkkálaga —Growing Stronger Together: Sámi Children's Communication Rights
abstract: Purpose: This viewpoint article examines how Sámi children are supported within the Norwegian education system. While Article 2 and Article 30 in the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child affirm Indigenous children's rights to language and culture, the question remains: What is required to ensure that the rights of Sámi children with speech, language, and communication needs are fully upheld in practice? This article explores whether current policies and practices ensure inclusion and cultural recognition for this group. Method: Using a viewpoint approach, this article critically reflects on national policy documents and existing research on Sámi education, with a focus on children with speech, language, and communication needs. Results: Norway has established strong legal and policy frameworks to support Sámi language and culture in education. Despite this, significant barriers remain in practice to fully reflect both individual and cultural identities for Sámi children, posing particular challenges for those with speech, language, and communication needs. Conclusions: Sámi perspectives are limited in special education, and mechanisms for including these children's

journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Misclassification of Emergent Bilinguals: Diagnostic Profiles and Policy Action for Speech-Language Pathologists
abstract: Purpose: In this clinical focus article, we illustrate the need for early identification and differentiation of emergent bilingual kindergarteners as English learners, students with developmental language disorder (DLD), both, or neither, given the intersection of different policies and practices in these populations. We discuss the importance of speech-language screening for bilinguals in kindergarten and call for state- and district-level policy changes to correctly distinguish each bilingual student's language and educational needs. Method: We evaluated the language skills of 24 kindergarten emergent Spanish–English bilinguals attending elementary schools in the greater Phoenix area. We analyzed language proficiency, language assessment, school placement, and home language questionnaires. Results: A little over half of the students (54.2%) were placed correctly based on our assessments; however, the remaining 11 students (45.8%) fell into the following three diagnostic profiles: (a) underidentification of DLD, (b) overidentification of DLD, and (c) overidentification of English learners. title: Exploring Spatial Hearing Abilities in Children With Bilateral Cochlear Implants Using Three-Dimensional Virtual Reality Systems
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to (a) examine the contribution of head movements to sound localization through a within-participant manipulation (i.e., movement vs. no-movement conditions) across all three groups (children with normal hearing and simultaneous and sequential bilateral cochlear implant users) and (b) compare sound localization performance across the three groups, with particular emphasis on the inclusion of two distinct groups of cochlear implant users (simultaneous and sequential bilateral cochlear implant users). Method: Twenty-one normal-hearing children and 14 children with simultaneous cochlear implants, as well as 18 children with sequential cochlear implants, aged 6–14 years, participated in the study. Three-dimensional hearing abilities were examined using virtual reality systems. Participants were evaluated in two listening conditions, head mobile and head immobile, at two distances (35 and 55 cm) and at four angles (right-front, +30°; left-front, −30°; right-back, +150°; left-back, −150°). journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Enhancing Clinical Practice Through Research: Tools for School-Based Speech-Language Pathologists
abstract: Purpose: Speech-language pathologists (SLPs) in the school setting need to efficiently locate, evaluate, and utilize research evidence in their clinical practice. This tutorial provides resources focused on the foundational aspects of evidence-based practice (EBP) and its application for SLPs to implement research into clinical practice. Method: This tutorial (a) reviews study design and discusses clinical questions best suited to each; (b) provides key tips for extracting information from main sections of research articles; (c) discusses the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) as a clinical and research tool, including actionable steps and examples for using AI in EBP; and (d) provides detailed strategies to increase interaction with research beyond reading articles. Results: School-based SLPs can utilize the information and strategies provided to increase their confidence in evaluating research literature, applying information, and incorporating resources from research articles into their clinical practice. Conclusions: This tutorial equips school-based SLPs with actionable steps and concrete tools to increase ease and efficiency of applying research evidence into clin

title: Comparing English-Speaking Third- Through Sixth-Grade Students' Performances on Spoken and Written Cloze Morphological Awareness Tasks
abstract: Purpose: Morphological awareness, the ability to consciously think about morphemes, plays an important role in literacy achievement. Historically, when measuring morphological awareness, researchers primarily have administered tasks in the spoken rather than written modality, and few have investigated the influence of modality on task performance. Thus, the purpose of this study was to determine whether performance on cloze morphological awareness tasks would be different for English-speaking third- through sixth-grade students depending on whether the task was administered in the spoken or written modality. We also analyzed whether performance on a written version explained unique variance on measures of word-level reading and spelling after controlling for receptive vocabulary and performance on the spoken morphological awareness task. Method: Third- through sixth-grade English-speaking students ( n > 150 per grade) in the United States completed cloze tasks measuring their awareness of base words and their inflected or derived forms, as well as standardized measures of real word reading, decoding, spelling, and receptive vocabulary. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: “An Unequal Two-Way Endeavor”: Building Harmonious Collaboration Between Itinerant Speech-Language Pathologists and Teachers
abstract: Purpose: This study explored how itinerant speech-language pathologists (SLPs) and school teachers in Taiwan collaborate to deliver effective speech-language therapy (SLT) within a teacher-centered model. Whereas school-based SLT in many Western contexts typically involves therapists embedded full-time within schools, Taiwan relies primarily on an itinerant service model in which SLPs travel across multiple schools with limited onsite presence. This structural difference requires intensive interprofessional coordination to support students with speech, language, and communication needs. Method: Using a phenomenological approach, semistructured interviews were conducted with 10 itinerant SLPs and 10 teachers who had established positive collaborative relationships. Data were analyzed through thematic analysis to identify shared characteristics and strategies that fostered effective collaboration. Reflexive procedures, double coding, and member checking enhanced analytic rigor and trustworthiness. Results: Three themes captured the essence of harmonious SLP and teacher collaboration: relationships evolving from shared goals to professional friendship; a three-partner waltz among SLPs

title: Examining Relationships Between Caregiver Concerns and Family and Child Characteristics in Kindergarten Children at Risk for Language and Literacy Disorders
abstract: Purpose: Identification of children with language impairments often relies on caregivers raising concerns. However, caregivers may find it difficult to identify language impairment. This study examined how child and family characteristics were related to the likelihood that caregivers reported concerns about oral language and literacy to understand the possible underlying factors influencing identification. Method: In a larger longitudinal study, kindergarten children ( N = 385) completed a battery of oral language and literacy assessments. The caregivers completed a questionnaire including demographic information (e.g., caregiver education level) and reported concerns in the areas of oral language, literacy, speech, and attention/memory. We used two multiple logistic regressions to evaluate the predictors of caregivers' concern about (a) oral language and (b) literacy. Results: Among the children with language difficulties, less than 40% of caregivers reported oral language concerns. Among the children with word reading difficulty, just over half of the caregivers reported literacy concerns. title: La Jaula de Oro : An Examination of Latinx Bilingual Adolescents' Translingual Practices and Language Outcomes in Critical Thinking and Complex Language Production
abstract: Purpose: This study uses a translanguaging orientation in assessment design. A translanguaging orientation adopts a poststructuralist view of multilingual practices. In the current application to measurement, we take a positivist approach, wherein we measure languages independently and general language use—or a translanguaging condition. In measuring “languaging practices,” we used this design to quantify Latinx adolescents' use of critical thinking language, language complexity, and productivity when they are translanguaging and discussing culturally situated narratives, corridos . Method: Fifty Latinx adolescents listened to and discussed Spanish corridos and English ballads in three different languaging conditions: closed Spanish, closed English, and translanguaging. Responses were audio-recorded, transcribed, and coded for indices of critical thinking language (i.e., metacognitive terms), language complexity (i.e., mean length of utterance in words, clausal density), and language productivity (i.e., total number of words and number of different words). journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Social Support Intervention Effects on Stress and Burnout in School-Based Speech-Language Pathologists
abstract: Purpose: Social support is an interpersonal resource with established effects on reducing occupational stress and burnout. Unlike typically recommended self-care and self-awareness techniques, social support can be directly implemented in the workplace and serves as an effective buffer against job-related stressors. This study aimed to determine how social support influences reported occupational stress and burnout symptoms among speech-language pathologists (SLPs). Method: We developed and implemented a social support group program called Peer Support for School-based Speech-Language Therapists, using a randomized control trial design. Forty-six school-based SLPs were randomly assigned to either an immediate or delayed treatment group and participated in weekly social support group sessions online for 6 weeks. Pretest, posttest, and delayed posttest scores on the SLP Stress Inventory and the Maslach Burnout Inventory: Educators Survey were compared. Results: Changes across postintervention and delayed postintervention for the treatment group were observed. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Integrating the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health Into Speech-Language Pathology Work With Children With Vision Differences
abstract: Purpose: Children and youth with vision differences, including those with low vision, blindness, or deafblindness, often experience communication challenges that impact their participation at home, in school, and in the community. These challenges can be complex and multidimensional, requiring thoughtful, individualized approaches to support communication and overall development. Method: This clinical focus article introduces the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), along with its version for children and youth, as a practical and holistic framework for supporting this population. We explore how specific relevant ICF categories align with the lived experiences of children with visual impairment or deafblindness and demonstrate their application in speech-language pathology assessment, goal setting, and intervention planning. Results: Drawing on the literature, we highlight the current challenges and promising opportunities for integrating the ICF into speech-language pathologists' (SLPs') everyday clinical practice. title: Can We Identify Struggling Writers in the Classroom Using Pseudowords?
abstract: Purpose: Early identification of literacy difficulties is essential to implement effective remediation strategies. Often, tests are time-consuming and may require expert practitioners to administer or interpret them. This study tested an easy-to-use spelling tool screen for early writing difficulties. Specifically, we explored whether a pseudoword spelling task was effective for the early identification of struggling writers (SWs). We examined its discriminatory ability and differences in performance as a function of item features. Method: Forty-eight primary SWs and 60 typically developing (TD) peers completed a pseudoword dictation task in Catalan (Pseudoword Spelling Evaluation in Catalan Language [PSE-CL]). We analyzed key psychometric properties of the task, including its reliability and discriminatory ability. Item manipulation allowed for an analysis between and within group performance based on item features (i.e., length and frequency of the original base word). Results: The task showed good internal consistency and reliability, with grade-specific variations. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Assessment of Personal Narrative Skills in Children Aged 4–18 Years: A Systematic Review
abstract: Purpose: Assessment of children's personal narratives offers important insights into their functional language abilities. This systematic review identifies current assessment and analysis practices for evaluating the personal event narratives of school-age children and provides a comprehensive overview to guide future research and clinical application. Method: The review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42022345679) and followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Electronic databases (CINAHL, ERIC, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, SCOPUS, and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global) were searched in August 2022 and September 2024 for peer-reviewed studies and dissertations or theses published in English that evaluated personal narrative skills in participants aged 4–18 years. There was no date limit. Extracted data included study design, participant samples, assessment tasks, and analysis measures. Analysis measures were categorized using the Linguistic Underpinnings of Narrative in Aphasia (LUNA) framework. Results: A total of 211 studies (37,477 participants) were included. title: Introduction to the Forum: Global Assessment of Narratives
abstract: Purpose: This article introduces the Forum: Global Assessment of Narratives, which brings together contributions highlighting two freely accessible narrative assessment tools developed for international and cross-linguistic use: Global TALES (Talking About Lived Experiences in Stories) for eliciting personal narratives, and LITMUS-MAIN (Language Impairment Testing in Multilingual Settings–Multilingual Assessment Instrument for Narratives) for eliciting fictional narratives. It summarizes how narrative-based approaches can enrich and enhance existing assessment practices and argues that narratives are an integral part of clinical assessment, as they allow for in-depth, multidimensional evaluation of an individual's spoken language skills. Method: We first provide a rationale for considering both personal narrative and fictional narrative assessment in clinical practice. Then, we outline the development of Global TALES and MAIN, including progress made in recent years. We end with a summary of the six articles in this forum, highlighting their clinical implications. title: Heritage Speakers Telling Fictional Stories in Two Languages: Cross-Linguistic Differences in Macrostructure
abstract: Purpose: The article aimed to examine cross-linguistic differences in macrostructure abilities in the narratives of 5- to 6-year-old preschool children from diverse heritage language (HL) backgrounds who speak Hebrew as the societal language (SL). Method: Data were collected from 104 preschool children (ages 5–6 years), bilingual speakers of English–Hebrew ( n = 34), Russian–Hebrew ( n = 50), and French–Hebrew ( n = 20). Narratives were collected via retelling in both languages with support from six colored pictures following the procedures and coding of the Language Impairment Testing in Multilingual Settings–Multilingual Assessment Instrument for Narratives (LITMUS-MAIN). Story scripts in each language reflect story grammar (SG) elements, including setting (time, place, and main characters) and three episodes per story, where each episode contains goal, attempt, and outcome. Stories retold in both languages were transcribed and coded for macrostructure features, following the LITMUS-MAIN coding procedure. journal_name: Language, Speech & Hearing Services in Schools
title: Temporal Processing and Literacy Skills in Children With Hearing Aids
abstract: Purpose: The aim of this study was to examine the relationship between temporal processing and literacy performance in children with hearing aids. Method: The study included a total of 45 children, comprising 21 with typical hearing and 24 who used hearing aids, all of whom were attending the second, third, or fourth grades of primary school. Temporal processing skills were evaluated using the Frequency Pattern Test and the Duration Pattern Test (DPT), whereas reading and writing abilities were assessed through the Literacy Assessment Battery. Results: Children using hearing aids demonstrated statistically significantly lower performance in the DPT and in the test assessing writing skills compared to their typically hearing peers. A positive, significant correlation was found between temporal processing skills and literacy skills. Moreover, temporal processing and literacy performance were observed to be negatively correlated with the age at which the child's first amplification was provided and positively correlated with the duration of auditory rehabilitation. title: Exploring Personal Narrative Coherence in 10-Year-Old Children: A Global Study Using the Global TALES Protocol
abstract: Purpose: The overall aim of this exploratory study was to evaluate personal narrative coherence in groups of children representing a range of cultural and/or linguistic backgrounds. Based on previous research, we expected to find effects based on culture/language participant group and the emotional valence of the prompt (positive, negative, neutral). We also anticipated potential interactions between culture/language participant group and prompt type. Method: Four hundred seventeen 10-year-old children from 21 culture/language participant groups took part in this cross-sectional study. The children were from 19 countries or regions, speaking 18 different languages or dialects. All children were seen individually, either face-to-face or online, and asked to produce personal narratives in response to the Global Talking About Lived Experiences in Stories (TALES) protocol. Three of their narratives, each representing a different emotional valence—happy, angry, and a problem situation—were included in the current study. title: Evaluating Childhood Apraxia of Speech in Cantonese-Speaking Children: A Tutorial Based on Available Evidence
abstract: Purpose: Recent research has increasingly focused on childhood apraxia of speech (CAS) in non–English-speaking populations, with Cantonese emerging as a significant language of study. This tutorial seeks to consolidate current knowledge regarding CAS in Cantonese speakers and proposes an assessment battery accompanied by observational criteria to support both clinical practice and research applications. Method: The proposed assessment battery includes five tasks: the Hong Kong Cantonese Articulation Test, a connected speech sample derived from a story retelling task, the Cantonese Oral and Speech Motor Assessment, the Imitation of Polysyllables task, and the Tone Sequencing Task (Version 3.2). Diagnostic criteria incorporate five key features observed across these tasks, supported by quantitative thresholds, reference values, and cutoff scores drawn from prior research. A modified version of the Profile of Childhood Apraxia of Speech and Childhood Dysarthria, tailored for Cantonese speakers, is also included to differentiate CAS from childhood dysarthria. title: A Scoping Review of the Effectiveness of Remote Microphones in Classrooms on Children's Listening, Learning, and Well-Being Applying the Listen to Learn for Life Assessment Framework
abstract: Purpose: The aim of this scoping review article was to understand the effectiveness of remote microphones in classrooms on listening, learning, and well-being for children aged 0–18 years. Method: This scoping review article followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews. The PICO (population, intervention, comparison, outcome) framework was used to outline the eligibility criteria. Web of Science, PsycInfo, MEDLINE, and PubMed were searched on November 17, 2025. Eligible studies were charted according to the population; the comparison (no device vs. device, device vs. device); the measure used to assess listening, learning, or well-being; the findings of the study; and the effect of the remote microphone on children's listening, learning, or well-being. Results: A total of 686 papers were returned in the search after removing duplicates. Of these, 66 papers met the criteria to be included in the review. Children with hearing loss was the most studied population, and listening was the most studied outcome. title: Mind the Gap: Understanding How a Speech-Language Pathologist's Grammar Knowledge Affects Assessment
abstract: Purpose: This study examined whether school-based speech-language pathologists (SLPs) could use their grammatical knowledge and the Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals–Fifth Edition (CELF-5) Formulated Sentences subtest manual to score responses accurately and consistently and to determine how scoring variability may influence potential eligibility outcomes. Method: Ninety-seven practicing school-based SLPs completed a 141-item online survey. The survey included demographic questions, self-ratings of grammatical knowledge and confidence, and three sets of Formulated Sentences responses from children aged 7, 8, and 10 years. Participants scored items using standardized CELF-5 criteria and rated their confidence in each decision. Group comparisons were conducted between SLPs who had completed language science coursework and those who had not. Results: Participants reported neutral to somewhat strong grammatical knowledge and confidence. Although SLPs with language science coursework had higher knowledge and confidence in assessing grammar, they did not demonstrate greater scoring accuracy.
